Breaking: The 22 Best European Christmas Markets to Visit This Winter

📅 01 Dec 2022 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2380 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vogue

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • There’s nothing quite like a Christmas market to set a joyful tone for the holiday season.
  • If you’re especially fortunate, you might even find yourself exploring a traditional European Christmas market this winter—a bucket list item for travelers with a proclivity for all things merry and bright.
  • But it’s hardly the only country that excels at this holiday event.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There’s nothing quite like a Christmas market to set a joyful tone for the holiday season. Is there anywhere else where it’s acceptable to mill about with a hearty mug of glögg in one hand, an even larger potato pancake in the other, while exceeding your budget on handcrafted ornaments and posing for photos in front of a wooden sleigh? The answer, we can confidently say, is no.

If you’re especially fortunate, you might even find yourself exploring a traditional European Christmas market this winter—a bucket list item for travelers with a proclivity for all things merry and bright. A natural place to start when curating an itinerary is Germany, and for good reason: It is, after all, the birthplace of the Christmas market, with Dresden’s Striezelmarkt first springing up all the way back in 1434.

But it’s hardly the only country that excels at this holiday event. There are numerous other destinations scattered across the continent—some familiar, and some wonderfully under the radar—that deliver the festive goods. Here, find 22 storybook European Christmas markets to make 2026 your most memorable holiday season yet.

What to Expect: The Stortorget Christmas Market is held in Gamla Stan, Stockholm’s old town, that dates back to the 13th century and is encircled by historic merchant houses. It’s often snowy this time of year, so enjoy the crunch of fresh powder beneath your feet as you meander medieval alleys and peruse the market’s 41 chalet-shaped stalls. If you’re hungry, pick up a smoked sausage or some lussekatter, a brioche-like saffron bun. You can cross everyone off your shopping list with the cozy selection of hand-knitted sweaters and traditional ornaments, all illuminated by the market’s endless strings of festive lights. (And speaking of light, if your visit to Stockholm happens to land on December 13, don’t miss Lucia, the country’s traditional, candlelit festival.).

Where to Stay: Lydmar Hotel (12-minute walk).

It has been revealed that what to Expect: The term ‘fairytale’ gets thrown around a lot when speaking of Christmas markets, but in the case of Wroclaw, it’s simply the best way to describe it. This magical atmosphere—complete with gothic architecture and a 75-foot-tall (artificial!) Norwegian spruce—stretches across four interconnected areas: the market square (Rynek), the salt square (Plac Solny), Świdnicka Street, and Oławska Street. While exploring, don’t miss the opportunity to try oscypek, a smoked cheese from the Polish mountains that is served with cranberries and best paired with a glass of mead (Poland’s oldest traditional alcoholic drink).

Where to Stay: Hotel Altus Palace (15-minute walk).

Location: Place des Dominicains, Place Jeanne d’Arc, Place de l’Ancienne Douanne, Koïfhus, Place des Six Montagnes Noires, and Square de la Montagne Verte.

When: Ends December 29 (though the Gourmet Market runs until January 3).

In a recent development, what to Expect: There are six (yes, six) total markets in this little town, which looks like the missing chapter of a fairytale book even when it’s not covered in string lights and fir branches. They’re all scattered around the Old Town and serve slightly different purposes: The main one on Place des Dominicains is mostly arts and crafts themed, with a few kids’ rides spread; the Place Jeanne d’Arc market is set up to look like a traditional Alsatian village; the Marché Gourmand at Square de la Montagne Verte is the spot for scrapings of creamy raclette, rich tartiflette, and hot cups of mulled wine.

Where to Stay: Relais & Châteaux La Maison Des Têtes (3-minute walk).

What to Expect: Dating back to the 17th century, the Nuremberg Christmas market (“Christkindlesmarkt”) is one of the first on the continent, and the city certainly goes all-out in homage to this tradition. Nicknamed the “city of wood and cloth,” it stands out for its candy cane-striped cloth tents, each housing glass tree baubles, fresh-baked gingerbread, and handmade wooden trinkets. Traveling with little ones? The children’s Christmas market is just around the corner on Hans-Sachs-Platz, and includes everything from a lit-up merry-go-round to a bake house where they can roll out their own dough.

Where to Stay: Karl August (one-minute walk).

Location: On Barfüsserplatz and Münsterplatz in the historic old town.

What to Expect: In Basel, around 155 rustic wooden chalets are set against the backdrop of the city’s old town, set aglow with glittering lights. A magnificent Christmas tree is erected in the historic center with ornaments by local decorating legend Johann Wanner, while stalls are bedecked in string lights and tinsel at every turn. After picking up a few artisanal gifts and goodies, head for the 13-meter-high Christmas pyramid on Barfüsserplatz for mulled wine, followed by a stroll along the Rhine River.

Where to Stay: Les Trois Rois (10-minute walk).

What to Expect: The Wiener Chriskindlemarkt und Weihnachtstraum Christmas market is perhaps the largest and well-known in Vienna, but with this precedent comes crowds. Instead, founder of bespoke travel organization Black Tomato Tom Marchant points to the Christmas village at the Belvedere Palace as an in-the-know, less-trafficked alternative preferred by locals; here, you can wander around the palace’s lavish 18th-century Baroque architecture while indulging in mulled wine and delectable pastries. “Lots of locally crafted jewelry can be found in this area,” indicates Marchant. “Scented woods, ceramics, wooden hats, decorations, drinking horns—it’s quite a stunning place.”.

Where to Stay: Miiro Spittelberg (20 minutes by tram).

Location: The Grande Île (Old Town).

Industry observers note that what to Expect: Known by holiday devotees as the “capital of Christmas,” Strasbourg is home to the oldest holiday market in France, dating all the way back to 1570. Visitors to this picturesque city in the Alsace region can pop in and out of 13 quaint markets, all within walking distance of each other in the old town. The original, however, is known as Christkindelsmärik and can be found at Place Broglie—there you, can sip on a mug of vin chaud while zipping around tinsel-adorned chalets in front of the Gothic cathedral.

Where to Stay: Hotel Cour du Corbeau Strasbourg-Mgallery (15-minute walk).

According to recent reports, what to Expect: Christmas markets and Germany are inextricably linked—it’s been estimated that there are over 2,500 in the country alone—and one of the best places to begin your exploration of the region’s holiday traditions is in the fairytale fortress town of Heidelberg. The historic city’s landscape includes the Neckar River and Odenwald Forest, while it also boasts architectural landmarks such as the Old Bridge and a prestigious 14th-century university attended by everyone from Hegel to Hannah Arendt. Heidelberg’s Christmas market is scattered throughout the illuminated storybook alleys of the old town, where the smell of roasted nuts wafts in the air as you dip into huts for souvenirs. Kids in tow? Go ice skating on Karlsplatz, or take a spin on the antique carousel.

Where to Stay: Heidelberg Suites House of Hütter (10-minute walk).

Where to Stay: Telegraaf Hotel (5-minute walk).

Location: East Princes Street Garden.

It has been revealed that what to Expect: With the unmistakable silhouettes of Edinburgh Castle and the Scott Monument in the distance, Edinburgh’s holiday market—located in the center of the Scottish city—imbues its ancient walkways with a lively charm. Take in bird’s eye views from atop the glittering ferris wheel or glide across the ice skating rink surrounded by 18th-century architecture. Afterward, trot around the cheery network of vendors serving Scottish delicacies and winter drinks, or pick up last-minute artisanal gifts and decorations at the market’s many boutique stalls.

Where to Stay: The Roseate Edinburgh (10-minute drive).

Location: Tivoli Gardens and Højbro Plads.

When: Ends January 3 and December 20, respectively.

What to Expect: Entering Copenhagen’s Tivoli Gardens during the holiday season feels like wandering into an undiscovered Nordic village. This 175-year-old theme park is transformed annually into a Christmas market with 60 stalls swathed in magical decor, including log cabins draped in pine cones and layers of snow—and that’s without mentioning the garden itself, which glows with over 70,000 Christmas baubles and 1,000-plus trees draped in lights. A 10-minute walk away, Højbro Plads also lures in visitors with 18,000 sparkling lights, plus live reindeer pulling a Santa’s sleigh.

Where to Stay: Villa Copenhagen (5 and 15-minute walk).

Industry observers note that what to Expect: If you’re looking for a more pastoral feel, head to the Cotswolds, England’s most romantic region of storybook countryside. “With quaint villages adorned in lights, caroling, and frequent dustings of snow, the Cotswolds evokes Christmas from the days of old,” Marchant notes. The ancient city of Bath sits on the region’s edge and is hosting the 20th anniversary of its annual holiday market this year. With over 150 stalls offering unique goods like pottery, hand-knit socks, artisan cheeses, and beyond, you’ll cross off your shopping list—and then some.

Where to Stay: Thyme (1-hour drive).

Location: Govone Castle and Asti’s historic center.

Recent findings suggest that what to Expect: Bordering France and Switzerland, Italy’s northern Piedmont region is a hotspot for wintry festivities—but the atmospheric Christmas markets of neighboring towns Govone and Asti are the real standout. In Govone, tucked away inside the 18th-century royal castle, is both the House of Santa Claus and an exhibition that timelines the city’s Christmas celebrations over the centuries. If you want to shop, however, nearby Asti is where you’ll find over 130 workstations of artisans and food and wine producers scattered across Italy; afterwards, visit the living nativity scene put on by nearly 100 local volunteers.

Where to Stay: Relais San Maurizio (30-minute drive).

What to Expect: If you ask Finns where Santa Claus comes from, they’ll proudly declare their country as the answer. (Lapland, to be precise.) This alone makes celebrating the holiday in the capital of Helsinki an exhilarating and celebratory affair. “This is one of the best holiday markets in Europe,” Marchant says. “The cathedral overlooks the Helsinki Christmas market, which has over 100 stalls and stands with hand-crafted gifts, ornaments, locally-grown produce, and fish and meats sourced hyper-locally.” What are you waiting for?

Where to Stay: Hotel Haven (5-minute walk).

According to recent reports, location: Vorosmarty Square and St. Stephen’s Basilica.

What to Expect: Brave the bone-chilling weather with a bowl of goulash soup or steaming chimney cake at Budapest’s beloved Christmas market located along the cobblestone streets of Vörösmarty Tér (Vorosmarty Square) in the heart of the city. About a 10-minute walk away you can also discover Christmas festivities in front of St. Stephen’s Basilica; the advent festival hosts around 100 craft exhibitors, an ice rink, and more. (It was named Best Christmas Market in Europe for three years in a row, if that sort of accolade piques your interest.).

Where to Stay: Four Seasons Hotel Gresham Palace Budapest (5-minute walk).

What to Expect: This century-old holiday fair has over 100 wooden stalls and is nestled in Madrid’s Plaza Mayor town square. The merrymaking vibes are cemented with a glowing carousel, nativity scenes (belénes), and loads of handcrafted ornaments and gifts to choose from. You can also savor seasonal Spanish flavors like churros con chocolate washed down with a cup of mulled wine.

Where to Stay: Rosewood Villa Magna (15-minute drive).

Location: Market Square and Simon Stevin Square.

Sources indicate that what to Expect: Appointed the whimsical title of Winter Glow, the annual festival in the medieval city of Bruges is nothing short of magical. Begin your visit on the light trail; a walk along 10 illuminated installations, all connected by a wintry blue glow. Then head for the Christmas markets for festivities that feel plucked from a fairytale. Technically there are two markets—one in the Market Square and the other in Simon Stevin Square—but as they are situated less than a five-minute walk from each other, it’s easy to do both. Peruse the atmospheric stalls for handcrafted decorations, wool socks, and plenty of Belgian treats and mulled wine, followed by a spin around the ice rink.

Where to Stay: Hotel Van Cleef (10-minute walk).

Location: Roßmarkt, along the Zeil, down to Römerberg, and to the Main River.

What to Expect: With origins dating back to the 14th century, the Frankfurt Christmas market is among the oldest in the world. As such, it’s also one of the most popular markets, attracting millions of festive guests each year and stretching across several parts of the old town. Meander through its many decorated stalls, make a pitstop at the tree in Römerberg square, and don’t forget to devour a bethmännchen (a marzipan pastry that is unique to Frankfurt and baked just for Christmas).

Where to Stay: Schlosshotel Kronberg (30-minute drive).

Location: Dom and Residenzplatz Square.

What to Expect: This traditional market is cozied up in the heart of Salzburg’s UNESCO World Heritage Site and has origins that go back to the late 15th century. These days, Christmas lovers descend upon the market’s 100-plus stands in search of Austrian specialties, festive incense aromas, traditional crafts, and decorations for the tree—all found within traditional huts.

Where to Stay: Rosewood Schloss Fuschl (30-minute drive).

Location: Old Town Square and Wenceslas Square.

It has been revealed that what to Expect: Soak up the magic of Czechia at Prague’s holiday market. Get into the spirit of the season as you hop from one decorated wooden hut to the next, purchasing artisan crafts and delectable treats along the way. Curious what you’ll be eating? Look to popular Czech dishes like šunka (significant hams roasted on spits), klobása (barbecued sausages), and rybí polévka (a traditional Christmas soup).

Where to Stay: Four Seasons Hotel Prague (10 to 20 minute walk).

It has been revealed that what to Expect: For those in search of something out of the ordinary, Valkenburg’s underground Christmas markets are a winning bet. The small southern Dutch town hits all the marks when it comes to setting the right tone for the season, but once you head into its caves and tunnels that’s when the magic truly begins. Bedecked in twinkly lights, these merry passages wind beneath castle ruins and offer stalls stocked with gifts and goodies. There’s even a cave with life-size sand sculptures and 3-D holiday paintings. Above ground, pay a visit to Santa’s Village, a more traditional market filled with chalets serving up hot drinks and Christmas trinkets.

According to recent reports, where to Stay: Château St. Gerlach (10-minute drive).

Where to Stay: Amerikalinjen (10-minute walk).

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that abercrombie & Fitch’s resurgence has been well documented, and the brand reveals no signs of slowing down. Alongside its familiar mix of timeless staples, contemporary silhouettes, and archival-inspired pieces, Abercrombie has introduced YPB, or Your Personal Best: a dedicated line of performance apparel designed to bring the same considered approach to the gym as it does to the rest of your wardrobe.

Comprising everything from tees and tanks to shorts and jackets, YPB reflects Abercrombie’s ability to evolve while staying true to its heritage. The collection makes a convincing case for performance wear that goes beyond the usual sea of uninspired basics and head-to-toe Lycra. It’s also versatile enough to seamlessly move from a strenuous workout to the everyday wardrobe rotation. To put the collection through its paces, we’ve styled three looks that show just how far YPB can go.

I am a chronic overheater so my gym outfits always reveal a bit of skin. (It’s also a vanity thing so I can see my muscles at work when I’m getting after it.) This vintage-inspired muscle tank looks like some of the actual vintage tees that I’ve taken a pair of scissors to without a stranger’s set-in stains. I have a lot of hair that gets in my way so headwear is a must when working out. A bandana is a nice throwback to the classic bodybuilder era and unlike a hat, it does a better job at soaking up the sweat so it’s not dripping down my face.

Industry observers note that the standout of this outfit is the shorts. Compression lined, they’re about as long as I’d go for shorts clocking in with a five-inch inseam. They have a discreet pocket in the liner to store my phone, and they're tight enough so my device doesn’t go flying out when I’m doing high knees. Plus, they’re stretchy enough for putting ass to grass on a squat without risking a NSFW tear between the cheeks.

Industry observers note that I’ve come to learn that recovery days are not only a blessing but a necessity. But they don’t necessarily mean you have to waste away on the couch all day. My active recovery days involve a lot of walking, and that means my workout shorts make an appearance once again. I can’t deny their comfort factor, and it’s hard to beat a sweater-and-shorts combo, an outfit beloved by my favorite A-listers.

The sweater was a quarter-zip with an elastic waistband for a more streamlined, tailored fit. And if I’m walking a little too briskly, the top easily comes off to reveal a staple graphic tee in my wardrobe.

Sources indicate that finally, I put on some pants! I don’t make it a habit to wear sweatpants out casually, but sometimes the weather calls for it. Hike ‘em up a bit and show off some crisp white socks, a style swerve I saw once and couldn’t help but copy.

The staple of this outfit is the heavyweight jacket. Its water-resistant lining keeps me dry when the meteorologists get the forecast wrong, and it’s lined to keep me warm as the days get shorter and the nights get longer. The two-way zipper also allows for some extra mobility, and it won’t bunch up when I sit down like so many other parkas.

KFC Franchisee Files For Bankruptcy With 84 Locations At Risk Of Closure

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that the future of 84 KFC and KFC/Taco Bell restaurants across 10 states is uncertain after one of the chain’s franchisees filed for bankruptcy.
  • In a recent development, the firm entered into franchise agreements in 2021 with KFC and Taco Bell, both owned by Yum!
  • In its bankruptcy filing, Tasty Chick’n notes that sales have declined by 15.6 percent over the past three fiscal years while operating costs have skyrocketed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the future of 84 KFC and KFC/Taco Bell restaurants across 10 states is uncertain after one of the chain’s franchisees filed for bankruptcy. The operator, Tasty Chick’n, filed for Chapter 11 protection in Texas on November 16.

In a recent development, the firm entered into franchise agreements in 2021 with KFC and Taco Bell, both owned by Yum! Brands. Tasty Chick’n’s portfolio includes 75 KFC restaurants and nine co-branded locations across Tennessee, Florida, Virginia, Arkansas, Kentucky, Illinois, Missouri, Alabama, Mississippi, and Indiana.

In its bankruptcy filing, Tasty Chick’n notes that sales have declined by 15.6 percent over the past three fiscal years while operating costs have skyrocketed. So far in 2026, restaurant-level profit margins have dropped to just 4 percent, down from 11 percent in 2023. And under its franchise agreements, nearly half of the franchisees’ locations require substantial and expensive upgrades through 2029.

Sources indicate that tasty Chick’n began deferring royalty payments in mid-2025 and generally stopped paying them altogether that November. This past September, KFC and Taco Bell’s franchising entities issued a notice of intent to terminate their agreements, claiming the operator owed nearly $16 million in unpaid royalties and other fees. Tasty Chick’n also faces approximately 14 lawsuits from landlords in five states over unpaid rent and other charges. The bankruptcy filing revealed that the operator has accrued nearly $73 million in funded debt.

The fate of the restaurants remains undecided. Tasty Chick’n is planning a court-supervised sale of its portfolio, either in its entirety or divided into different regional markets. Whether buyers will bite is another story, especially given KFC’s overall trajectory. A report earlier this year revealed that KFC had shuttered more than 300 locations between July 2025 and July 2026 alone.

No matter what happens to these KFC locations, this bankruptcy is another reminder of just how tough 2026 has been for fast food operators.

Mussels With Garlicky Miso Broth

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The seafood counter at your supermarket should sell rinsed and debarred mussels, but it’s easy to do at home.
  • More seafood dinners this way: Avgolemono Seafood Stew; Spaghetti alle Vongole; and Gorgeous Green Shrimp.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that mussels deserve your attention on weeknights. An affordable and accessible protein, they also happen to cook in less time than it takes to boil water. As the bivalves steam, they release a briny liquid, further perfuming the buttery, sake-fortified miso broth. Load up each bowl with a few good ladles, slurping every drop with an assist from crusty bread or warm rice. And why not enjoy the rest of the bottle of sake alongside your meal?

The seafood counter at your supermarket should sell rinsed and debarred mussels, but it’s easy to do at home. Discard any with cracked shells. Gently tap open raw mussels on a counter to see if they slowly close; if they do, those are okay to use. Swish them in a water-filled salad spinner or colander fitted inside a bowl, draining and refilling until water runs clear (give any especially dirty ones a scrub with a sponge). Use a towel to pull off the fibrous beard and set on a towel-lined tray in the fridge until you’re ready to cook.

More seafood dinners this way: Avgolemono Seafood Stew; Spaghetti alle Vongole; and Gorgeous Green Shrimp.

Place 2 Tbsp. scallions from 8 scallions, thinly sliced on a diagonal, in a small bowl and set aside for serving.

Melt 6 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a large pot over medium heat. Add 8 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and remaining scallions to pot and cook, stirring often, until softened, about 4 minutes. Add 2 Tbsp. white miso paste and ½ tsp. crushed red pepper flakes (if using) and cook until miso is broken up and incorporated into butter, about 20 seconds. Pour in 1 cup dry sake or dry white wine and stir to combine, then add 3–3½ lb. mussels, scrubbed, debearded. Cover pot and increase heat to medium-high. Cook, shaking pot occasionally, until mussels open, 5–7 minutes (discard any that do not open). Remove pot from heat.

It has been revealed that squeeze 1 lemon half over mussels. Cut remaining 1 lemon half into wedges for serving. Taste broth and season with kosher salt if needed.

Ladle mussels and broth among shallow bowls, then scatter reserved scallions over. Serve with country-style bread or steamed white rice if desired and lemon wedges for squeezing over.

25 Best Airbnbs in Paris 2026 for a Stylish Sojourn in the City of Light

📅 28 Jun 2021 | ⏱️ 18 min read (3675 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vogue

⏱️ ~18 mins left to finish

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When you book something through our retail links, we may earn an affiliate commission.

There are two sorts of Parisian holidays. The first, an exercise in blissful escapism, where luxury hotels, gallery hopping, and lazy apéros à la terrasse all help you lean into the romantic undercurrent of the city. The second, an exercise in make-believe: You would not be the first person to plot a move to Paris halfway through your stay there, earmarking local boulangeries and wine shops as favorites and spending mornings chit-chatting with market vendors. If you lean toward the latter experience, this is where the best Airbnbs in Paris enter the picture. After all, what better way to cosplay a Parisienne than via a cozy flat of your own (albeit a temporary one)?

Industry observers note that our edit is an evolving one—there’s no shortage of stately Haussmann buildings available for rent—grouped by arrondissement. (There are 20 total, and while we haven’t hit on all of them, the below list includes several of the most popular for visitors.) Each spot has its own distinct flair, depending on what sort of Parisian you wish to embody. The chichi traveler with high-brow tastes will love the classic charm of the Left Bank; the arty fashion-lover will prefer the cozy studios of the Marais (as well as its proximity to some of the best vintage shops); the low-key bohemian will find respite in the hills of Montmarte, above the city’s lights. Grand architecture and bistro balconies, you’ll be glad to discover, have no loyalty to any particular arrondissement. They’re all good; you really can’t go wrong.

For anyone planning a trip to the City of Light, consider the roundup of properties ahead for a true immersive experience in one of the most stylish cities on the planet.

According to recent reports, for a grand apartment right in the middle of the historical center, book this ornate Airbnb. Travelers looking to see all the sights will appreciate its proximity to the Palais Royal, Centre Pompidou, and the Louvre; it’s also around the corner from the Les Halles shopping center, where you’ll find both great restaurants (Le Petit Bouillon Pharamond is a nice option for an affordable lunch and gorgeous interiors) and little shops (E. Dehillerin, Julia Child’s much-frequented kitchenware store, is a must). The home itself is no less impressive—high ceilings with crown molding, antique gilded mirrors, and parquet floors run throughout.

Rooms: 2 bedrooms, 2 bathrooms; sleeps 4.

Amenities: Bathtub, washer, indoor fireplace, long-term stays allowed, elevator.

Exposed beams and parquet flooring set the scene for this typically charming Parisian apartment. There’s lots of space for making yourself right at home, including a stunning balcony that sits atop Rue de Rivoli so you’ll feel like you’re right in the middle of everything as you sip your morning espresso while mapping out the day’s itinerary. Then there’s the location: If it’s your first time visiting Paris, the fact that the Louvre museum, the Centre Pompidou, and the Seine are all within walking distance will be a massive bonus. Leave the complicated commutes for your sophomore outing; this home lets you walk everywhere.

Rooms: 2 bedrooms, 2.5 bathrooms; sleeps 4.

Amenities: Bathtub, washer/dryer, blackout shades, Devialet Bluetooth sound system, television, air conditioning, kitchen, dishwasher, espresso machine, balcony, housekeeping available at a cost.

Best for: First-timers to the city.

In a recent development, this sun-drenched two-bedroom near the Seine opens with a grand, golden-colored lobby, complete with a spiral staircase and tile floors. Upstairs, the duplex has lots of space to stretch out, from a dining table that doubles as a workspace to a bright living room to a small balcony. You’ll have both the fifth and sixth floors—but as there’s no elevator, prepare to get your cardio in. It’s in a fun area, too; Pizzeria Popolare, a great Italian restaurant, is just down the street, and you’re within easy exploring distance of all the boutiques and galleries the Marais has to offer.

Rooms: 2 bedrooms, 1 bathroom; sleeps 4.

Amenities: Bathtub, washer/dryer, Bluetooth sound system, television, balcony, pets allowed.

Best for: A small group of friends—who still want their own space.

Recent findings suggest that we’d book this Airbnb for the tiles alone. From the rainbow-colored bathtub to the celery green kitchen to the traditional tomettes that run throughout, it’s an effortlessly charming spot, located on the third floor of an 18th-century building. The enviable design continues from the baby blue bedroom to the painted furniture; it’ll be more than obvious that you’re staying in one of the more creative, artistic quartiers of the city. (And if you want to get some of your own work done, the dedicated office area is happy to oblige.) While it’s in a bustling neighborhood, the apartment itself is at the back of the property, so you’ll have quiet when you need it.

Rooms: 2 bedrooms, 1.5 bathrooms; sleeps 3.

Amenities: Bathtub, elevator, coffee maker, building staff.

In a recent development, if you picked the Marais because of its art scene, you might as well commit to the experience and book an Airbnb directly overlooking the Picasso Museum. Sought-after location aside, this duplex feels welcoming from the moment you step in the door. Hexagonal terracotta tiles line the floor, a large dining table is the perfect spot for a cozy night in, and every nook and cranny is filled with glass vases and art. When you want to head out for dinner, you’re spoilt for choice—but start with Chez Nenesse, a classic, red-and-white checkered tablecloth bistrot, that’s just four minutes away.

Rooms: 1 bedroom, 1 bathroom; sleeps 2.

Amenities: Kitchen, washer, Bose sound system, indoor fireplace, coffee maker.

The first thing this Airbnb has going for it is its location: It’s situated right on the Île Saint-Louis, one of the city’s two islands, and therefore has a more quaint feel to it than some of the busier arrondissements. (Plus you’re just five minutes from Berthillon, the best ice cream in the area.) The second thing, of course, is its style. The building itself is listed as a historic monument dating back to the 17th century, and interior highlights like a painted ceiling and gilded mirror amplify the antique appeal. Even the piano area, a tiny nook off one of the bedrooms, has a blue marble floor and matching tile mural—it’s all extremely decadent.

Rooms: 3 bedrooms, 2 bathrooms; sleeps 6.

Amenities: Washer/dryer, piano, indoor fireplace, parking, hot tub.

According to recent reports, we found your Parisian tree house. Tucked away near the busy Place des Vosges, the fourth-floor apartment is a calm respite, well-sized for a couple or solo traveler in search of more unique accommodation. Here, rustic wood beams accent nearly every ceiling and wall, textured brick flooring adds warmth, and a large, tiled tub looks out onto Haussmannian rooftops for a truly cozy stay. It even has two balconies—sure, they may be tiny, but the sweeping views of the city’s architecture more than makes up for their size.

Rooms: 1 bedroom, 1 bathroom; sleeps 3.

Amenities: Washer, television, piano, balcony, bathtub.

Best for: Those looking for a non-traditional vacation rental.

A bedroom adorned in pink toile de Jouy print, a working fireplace in the living room, a dining room that’s overflowing with plants and dressed up with a gilded mirror: this apartment, to borrow some first-level French, is très chic. It’s deceptively spacious—thanks to a sofa bed, it can actually sleep up to six people—making it ideal for a girls’ trip to the city. With a spacious living area and a well-equipped kitchen, it’s certainly designed to handle a larger group. A nice bonus? You’re within walking distance of the beloved bookstore Shakespeare and Company for a souvenir you can employ on the long flight home.

Rooms: 2 bedrooms, 1 bathroom; sleeps 6.

Amenities: Kitchen, TV, fireplace, washer/dryer, bathtub.

Steps away from the bustling Odéon neighborhood and landmarks like the Pantheon and the Luxembourg Garden, this apartment is ideally situated for first-timers to the city of lights. With original 1930s features preserved and played up, it's also well-decorated: Art Deco details, like geometric borders, curved ceiling cut-outs, and arched doorways pop up throughout. (The turquoise bathtub nook is a particular highlight; the glass wall in the dining room is another.) This rental has tons of space for a family as well as several kid-friendly amenities available upon request; book it for a longer stay in the city.

Rooms: 3 bedrooms, 2 bathrooms; sleeps 6.

Amenities: Bathtub, washer/dryer, piano, Bluetooth sound system, exercise equipment, television, high chair, board games, elevator, parking, pets allowed.

Location: By the Pantheon and the Luxembourg Garden.

Best for: Art Deco aficionados.

This literary, light-filled Airbnb is located in a building that houses several artists studios—notes of which can be found everywhere from the airy, industrial-style layout to the perfectly imperfect collection of decor to the multi-colored tiles in the kitchen. (As for the literary tie-in: Bookworms will appreciate the massive wall of books in the upstairs bedroom. Take your pick.) The home is mere blocks away from the Jardin du Luxembourg, in Montparnasse. Browse the aforementioned bookshelf and grab a paperback, pick up a coffee from one of the many cafés in the area, and take a morning to yourself in the gardens.

Rooms: 1 bedroom, 1 bathroom; sleeps 4.

Amenities: Kitchen, washer/dryer, TV, crib, courtyard.

Location: Near Jardin du Luxembourg.

Best for: Avid readers always looking for a new, picturesque spot to get lost in a book.

For the solo traveler who never wants to be too far from the sparkling lights of the Eiffel Tower, this little studio is a cozy cocoon just six minutes away. (Starting quite literally with the bed, which is cordoned off from the rest of the space by a chic glass wall and a gauzey curtain.) A tiny kitchenette stocked with all the essential appliances lets you make the most of local treats—helpful, as the famous Rue Cler street market is just around the corner, so you can stock up on cheeses, quiche, and even rotisserie chickens for quiet meals at home.

Rooms: 1 bedroom, 1 bathroom; sleeps 3.

Amenities: Washer, elevator, pet-friendly, housekeeping available at a fee.

Location: On Rue Amélie, a quick walk to the Eiffel Tower.

Best for: Foodies traveling alone.

It’ll be hard to beat this central location: This sunny, spacious two-bedroom is situated directly at the base of the Champ de Mars, the grassy park that houses the Eiffel Tower. It’s as stately as its zip code implies—think, period-appropriate wall moldings that reflect its 19th-century origins and oversized windows, with the occasional unexpected pop of color (like a yellow window in the kitchen and pistachio dining chairs) to keep it from feeling stuffy. It also comes with an espresso machine, so if you ever tire of your local boulangerie—unlikely—you can start the day with coffee at home.

Rooms: 2 bedrooms, 1.5 bathrooms; sleeps 3.

Amenities: Bathtub, washer, elevator.

Location: At the foot of the Eiffel Tower.

Best for: Ticking the Eiffel Tower off your bucket list.

Recent findings suggest that it’s conveniently located in the heart of Paris and stocked with modern creature comforts like a Nespresso machine and a Netflix-enabled television, but you really only need one reason to book this apartment: the massive terrace. Equipped with outdoor dining and seating, it’s a rare thing to find in the busy city (and, should you ever want a little quiet, an ideal spot to enjoy an apéro at home). Though it only has one proper bedroom, it can actually sleep four thanks to a sofa bed in the living room. For families looking for a comfortable spot near all the top sights, this is a great option.

Rooms: 1 bedroom, 1 bathroom; sleeps 4.

Amenities: Washer, blackout shades, HDTV, Bose sound system, exercise equipment, travel crib, kitchen, Nespresso coffee maker, dishwasher, terrace, paid parking available.

Location: In the Champs-Elysées area.

Best for: Travelers for whom a terrace with a view is a non-negotiable.

Sources indicate that staying in this palatial sixth-floor penthouse will feel like time travel—it sits within a historic Haussmann building and offers original details like 18th-century wood floors, hand-painted wallpaper, antique fireplaces, and a Napoleon-style oval room. It’s bourgeois luxury in every sense. The entire space enjoys plenty of light thanks to French windows opening onto three balconies, and amenities like a full kitchen and entry hall with a piano will make it difficult to venture outside (though you’ll want to—it’s in close proximity to some of Paris’s most coveted attractions like the Louvre, Opera Garnier, Champs Élysées).

Rooms: 4 bedrooms, 2 bathrooms; sleeps 8.

Amenities: Washer/dryer, piano, kitchen, elevator, balcony, antique fireplaces.

Location: In the Champs Elysées district.

Best for: Anyone who knows what a “Napoleon-style oval room” is (interior design buffs, this one’s for you).

Recent findings suggest that on the fifth floor of a traditional Haussmann building (there is an elevator, don’t worry) sits this elegant sunny spot. A long balcony stretches outside and includes a small bistro set for breakfasts outside—though the spacious dining room is also an enticing option. From the red-and-cream checkerboard kitchen to the ornate crown molding in the living area, it’s endlessly charming. Montmartre is only 15 minutes away; perhaps more importantly, depending on what your itinerary priorities are, the famous bakery Mamiche is an even-shorter 10 minute walk. (The brioche and the ham sandwich alone are good reasons to make a daily pilgrimage there each morning.).

Rooms: 4 bedrooms, 2 bathrooms; sleeps 5.

Amenities: Bathtub, washer, sound system, board games, fire place, balcony, elevator.

Best for: Design inspiration and proximity to an incredible bakery.

Recent findings suggest that originally belonging to the painter Georges Braque back in 1911, this sweet studio has since been re-done and can now fit up to four guests (the sofa converts to a bed, if you don’t mind a slightly crowded living space). The renovation didn’t strip it of its character, though, and between the primary-colored kitchen storage cubbies and the floor-to-ceiling windows that let the light stream in, it’s one of the more unique apartment rentals in Paris. The bay windows look out onto a courtyard, so you’ll have plenty of peace despite being located in one of the city’s most bustling areas for nightlife.

Rooms: 1 bedroom, 1 bathroom; sleeps 4.

Amenities: Washer/dryer, kitchen, shared backyard, coffee maker, crib/travel crib/children’s books available upon request, balcony.

Location: In the Pigalle neighborhood.

Best for: Those hoping to experience the city’s artistic spirit beyond a visit to the Louvre.

According to recent reports, right below Pigalle on Rue Cadet, this quiet one-bedroom is surrounded by bakeries, cheese shops, and greengrocers. Everything you’d need is within walking distance; head to Racines, a hole-in-the-wall Italian spot with a decadent tiramisù, for a date night in the neighborhood. Inside, a fully equipped kitchen and multiple workspaces ensure you have all the essentials to stretch out and make this temporary spot feel like home. With sloping ceilings and views onto the city’s greyscale rooftops, it feels like the coziest attic—peaceful, personal, and chic enough to make you want to stay awhile.

Rooms: 1 bedroom, 1 bathroom; sleeps 2.

Amenities: Washer, kitchen, dishwasher, coffee maker.

Location: In the Grand Boulevards area.

Best for: A cozy couples getaway.

If you can’t pick between the trendy 10th or 3rd arrondissements—don’t. This bright and airy one-bedroom is smack in the middle, in an ideal area full of hole-in-the-wall eateries and stylish spots to grab an apéro before a late dinner. Since it’s owned and designed by an architect, its interiors are especially appealing: The blend of vintage furniture and flourishing greenery might just inspire you to redecorate when you get home. In the meantime, you’ll feel right at home. The kitchen is significant enough to whip up meals of your own, if you feel inspired—or at least, a quick breakfast before heading out for the day.

Rooms: 1 bedroom, 1.5 bathrooms; sleeps 2.

Amenities: Bathtub, washer, blackout shades, HDTV, Apple sound system, piano, kitchen, dishwasher, Nespresso coffee maker.

Location: Right on the border of the 10th and the 3rd arrondissements.

Best for: Bookmarking design inspiration.

Recent findings suggest that overlooking the rooftops of Paris, this small but well-appointed apartment (yes, it has an elevator) is perfect for a couple. From a zellige-tiled kitchen to a teeny balcony where you can sip a cocktail during golden hour, you’ll find everything you need for a short stint in the city. But the best part is, hands down, its location: The home is right by the Canal. Here, you’ll find a livelier, younger scene, with natural wine bars, trendy restaurants, and an atmosphere that feels decidedly removed from the touristy center. (Early June, a local-favorite restaurant and wine bar with a rotating cast of guest chefs, is a leisurely 15-minute walk away.).

Rooms: 1 bedroom, 1 bathroom; sleeps 2.

Amenities: Washer, balcony, kitchen.

Sources indicate that location: Near the Canal St. Martin.

Best for: Proximity to your latest favorite wine bar.

For a vacation rental that feels designed by someone’s French grandma, choose this colorful, eclectic spot and make yourself at home. The kitchen, with its checkerboard-covered table, citron walls, and collected jumble of various tools and trinkets, is undoubtedly the center; but the bedrooms (there are three), with their massive windows and original terracotta floors are also nice—especially if you’re traveling with a substantial group, and want to make sure you each have enough space. When you do want to dine out, you’ll be well-positioned: Bistrot des Tournelles and Chez Paul, two wonderful traditional bistros, are located in this neighborhood.

Rooms: 3 bedrooms, 2 bathrooms; sleeps 5.

Best for: Cosplaying Julia Child for the weekend.

Recent findings suggest that not all Parisian Airbnbs involve ornate crown moldings and baroque antiques; some, like this loft, can lean quite industrial. Iron beams and high ceilings make it seem even more spacious (the space itself is located in an old printing house); glass windows overlook an internal courtyard, if you need a quiet temporary home. Sandwiched between République and Canal St. Martin, it’s in a fun, more local part of the city. If it’s warm enough, walk along the water in the afternoon before ducking into Chambre Noir, a little wine bar near the apartment, for small plates and a crisp glass of white.

Rooms: 2 bedrooms, 1 bathroom; sleeps 4.

Amenities: Bathtub, washer/dryer, TV, air conditioning, pet-friendly.

Best for: Fans of industrial architecture.

This two-bedroom apartment may just house the best balcony in all of Paris. It’s well-furnished, with plenty of potted plants and a bistro set for taking your breakfast outside, weather-permitting, but the views of the Haussmann buildings and Eiffel Tower in the distance are what makes it really special. Inside, the design is cozy, with floral quilts and Art Deco-inspired lighting casting everything in a warm glow. Even the entrance to the apartment is special. While the fifth floor rental is accessible by elevator, you may just find yourself choosing to take the stairs, which are lined with stained glass windows.

Rooms: 2 bedrooms, 2 bathrooms; sleeps 4.

Amenities: Washer/dryer, Sonos Bluetooth sound system, indoor fireplace, air conditioning, coffee maker, balcony, outdoor furniture, elevator.

Best for: Morning coffee on the balcony.

Perched in the heart of Montmartre in the hilly, cobblestone-lined streets of the Abbesses neighborhood, this one-bedroom home is ideal for the couple who likes their decor collected, full of personality, and a tiny bit mismatched. Starting with the mix of antique furnishings in the living room (including a red velvet armchair) and going right through to the lemon-yellow bedroom, the design of this place will make you feel like you’re visiting your artistic Parisian friend—no cold, white-box rooms here. When you do want to hit the tourist spots, the Basilica of Sacré Coeur is just a 15-minute walk away.

Rooms: 1 bedroom, 1 bathroom; sleeps 2.

Best for: The eclectic traveler coming to Paris to peruse the flea markets.

According to recent reports, you’re alone in Paris, and you need an inspiring studio from which to focus on your creative project (or just finish your book in peace): This artist’s loft is it. Tall ceilings and an oversized window create a light-filled environment, while a dedicated workspace offers a quiet place to concentrate. There’s a small but well-appointed kitchen so you can cook your meals at home and truly feel at ease during your stay, however long it may be.

Rooms: 1 bedroom, 1 bathroom; sleeps 4.

Amenities: Washer, crib, coffee maker, shared backyard.

Best for: Anyone coming to Paris to get out of a creative rut.

From the terracotta tomettes to the oversized windows, this sunny one-bedroom is perfect for the solo traveler or a couple. The building dates back to the 19th century, but the decor is firmly 21st: Butter yellow bedding and a mustard-striped kitchen skirt are design ideas to bookmark for when you get home. And you can’t trump the location: It’s right in the heart of Montmartre, only a few blocks away from Boulangerie Raphaëlle (one of the all-time best bakeries in the city—trust us).

Rooms: 1 bedroom, 1 bathroom; sleeps 2.

Amenities: Travel crib available upon request, coffee maker.

Best for: An extended solo trip.

In a recent development, jeans and ballerinas are the unofficial uniform of the city (and, conveniently, make a comfortable ensemble for a day of shopping). Bring an extra-large tote as your personal item on the plane so you have plenty of space to shuttle back all your souvenirs… including some French pharmacy goodies, of course.

After combing through hundreds of listings in a destination’s most desirable neighborhoods, we narrow down our list by reviewing a variety of determining factors, from the logistics of price, location, and amenities, to key details such as reviews and host information. From there, we take into consideration aesthetic details such as design, natural light, and overall look and feel of the home. The final edit is a well-rounded list that ensures booking a stay will result in a safe and stylish holiday.

Cecilie Bahnsen Rethinks the Fleece for Her Second Uniqlo Collaboration

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (676 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Elle

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor.
  • Sources indicate that cecilie Bahnsen has a cult following for a reason: the Danish designer’s big blooming dresses and dedication to sporty, easy balletcore have been collected in droves by fashion far and wide.
  • It has been revealed that for the occasion, Bahnsen spent half a year designing the collection and also collaborated with her friend Fumiko Imano, the artist, to shoot the campaign in Sweden amidst a picturesque landscape.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Sources indicate that cecilie Bahnsen has a cult following for a reason: the Danish designer’s big blooming dresses and dedication to sporty, easy balletcore have been collected in droves by fashion far and wide. So when Uniqlo came calling for her to design a second collaboration, it was time again for the designer to take the reins and merge her playful girlish Scandi style with the utilitarian wearability of the Japanese giant. The collection, which includes womenswear and childrenswear, puts a focus on cozy winter wardrobe dressing and is available now. In it, Bahnsen is rethinking and retooling the classic winter fleece.

It has been revealed that for the occasion, Bahnsen spent half a year designing the collection and also collaborated with her friend Fumiko Imano, the artist, to shoot the campaign in Sweden amidst a picturesque landscape. “It was very much about sisterhood, the journey you do of exploring together, and inspiration also from when I’m in the countryside with my son, and we collect flowers, and how we kind of, he sometimes pinned them on his jumper,” Bahnsen tells ELLE of the new collection. “I think it was really kind of that romantic or nostalgic feeling that I wanted to put into the collection. And then there was also this notion of just working with one fabrication and working with the fleece for winter and how you can work this as layering.”.

While Bahnsen in particular is known for her flouncy babydoll dresses, when it came to her second collection for Uniqlo, she tells us it was all about “refinement and balance and creating beautiful kind of everyday pieces.” Her personal favorite piece of the lineup is the fleece in the palest shade of soft pastel pink, embroidered with small flowers. “For me, the fleece is such a classic layering piece,” she notes. She’s already been wearing it herself for countryside outings. “There’s romance and nostalgia to pink, and I think with this collaboration, it was nice to do the fleece in pink,” she says. “Showing that it could have that femininity to it was special, and it is also that right tone as a super soft pink that I love.”.

The entire collection is designed to be layered, and the fleece is at the center of it. There’s a cropped fleece vest, a sheer long T-shirt printed with subtle bouquets of flowers, a floral-embellished fleece skirt and matching socks, gloves, and hats. Bahnsen herself recommends taking a cue from her own runway reveals. “I always love a substantial jumper or a big fleece over a poof-y dress,” she notes. “It has both a super boyish vibe to it but also a princess-y, romantic feeling, too, so I love those kinds of contrasts between each other.”.

Recent findings suggest that “These are pieces that you want to not just to work for one season, but to be timeless; it’s become about the perfection of these small details that makes it unique and maybe more romantic than what is normally in the Uniqlo collection,” adds Bahnsen. “I feel like the palette has a really Scandinavian winter tone to it, so how do you balance this soft pink into the darker blacks and blues, and kind of build it up, not in a monocomatic way, but really putting the tones and the layering together.” It’s definitely a chicer way to stay warm. The designer’s latest is the ultimate study of form and function.

Recent findings suggest that delish editors handpick every product we feature. We may earn commission from the links on this page.

In a recent development, the day before Thanksgiving is getting even more epic than usual. On November 25, Hershey’s is traveling back in time to when the company first released its iconic Milk Chocolate Bars. Back in 1900, the bars sold for just five cents a piece, and for one day only, the company is bringing back that original price.

Timed to coincide with the November 25 release of Hershey, a film about founder Milton Hershey starring Finn Wittrock and Alexandra Daddario, the super-discounted chocolate bars make for the perfect stocking stuffer or post-Thanksgiving treat.

There are a few ways to score the deal, although the rules vary depending on where you're shopping. Starting at 9 a.m. EST, customers can purchase the five-cent chocolate bars through Walmart.com for online pickup with a Walmart account. The offer is also available in stores through the Ibotta app, where shoppers must first purchase a bar at regular price and submit their receipt to receive cash back. Both options have a five-bar limit per person.

The bars will also be available through Amazon Grocery for same-day delivery where available. Hershey's will also share a promo code on its social channels for free shipping to qualifying addresses. Amazon purchases are limited to two bars per person, and additional fees for non-Prime members and taxes may apply.

In a recent development, lucky visitors to Hershey's Chocolate World in Hershey, Pennsylvania, and Times Square in New York City can also enjoy the deal, starting at 9 a.m. and 10 a.m., respectively. Purchases at these locations are limited to 10 bars per person while supplies last, and taxes may apply.

The Best Drip Coffee Makers, Test Kitchen Vetted & Editor Approved (2026)
